s: Scotland (a constituent country of the United Kingdom)
Schottland.et: From Middle High German Schottelant, Schotelant, Schotenlant. By surface analysis, Schotte (“Scot”) + -n- + Land (“land”).

Schote.et:
From Middle High German schōte (“pod; pea”), perhaps from Proto-Germanic *skaudō (“sheath, husk”), which is probably related to *hūdijaną (“to conceal”).
Cognate with Middle Low German schōde, Old Norse skauð, and perhaps the first element in Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐍂𐌰𐌹𐍀…
Unknown. Compare Zote (“salacious anecdote or joke”).

Schotter.et: From dialectal Central German, akin to German Schutt (“rubble, debris”), German schütten (“to pour, spill, cast, strew”).

Schotte.et: From Middle High German Schotte, Schote. Probably from Old English Sċott, perhaps borrowed through Middle Dutch Scotte. In any case, ultimately from Latin Scōtus.
From Middle High German schotte, from Old High German scotto, from Latin excoctus (“boiled”). Cognate with Italian scotto.

s: Scottish Gaelic (the Gaelic language of Scotland)
gates, borders, hatches (metaphorical dividers between a situation and an actor, preventing damage or influence)
Die Schotten sind dicht: Das Urteil ist rechtskräftig.
The gates are closed: The judgment is final.
Angesichts einer illegalen Einwanderungswelle macht das Land seine Schotten dicht.
Facing an illegal immigration wave, the country is closing its borders.
Schott.et: Borrowed from Low German Schot in the 18th century, from Middle Low German schot, ultimately from the root of schießen (“to shoot”). Cognate with Dutch schot.

Schottenrock.et: From Schotte (“Scotsman”) + -n- + Rock. The latter word probably in the sense of “skirt”, though it formerly also referred to various men’s garments (jacket, robe, uniform).
